findings.statement: per-segment blooms recover only part of the fan tax at sixteen segments
findings.detail: bloom16 keeps 82.1% of k1, between fan16's 48.5% and oracle16's 120.3% (vs fan bloom16 vs fan16: greater 1.693x (p=0.0022, rel_iqr 6.3%/8.5%); vs oracle bloom16 vs oracle16: less 0.683x (p=0.0022, rel_iqr 6.3%/1.6%)). A fixed probe order pays ~8.5 filter queries per lookup before its first data probe, which is why a per-segment filter cannot reach the ceiling at this k

findings.statement: a global key->segment map recovers at least 95% of perfect routing
findings.detail: route16 at 765ns/read against oracle16's 472 (route16 vs oracle16: less 0.617x (p=0.0022, rel_iqr 5.6%/1.6%)), 61.7% of the ceiling and 74.2% of k1. One hash lookup buys what sixteen filters cannot; the price is the one concession to global mutable state the next engine makes, and this is the number that justifies it

findings.statement: min/max fences prune nothing when segment key-ranges overlap
findings.detail: fence16 1274ns/read against fan16 1170 (fence16 vs fan16: NO DIFFERENCE (ratio 0.918, p=0.0553) -- within noise, not a result). Round-robin dealing makes every segment's range cover every key, so the fence admits every probe; recorded so the design never assumes fences route without key-partitioned sealing

notes: six arms interleaved in one process over two builds (one store, k segments, keys dealt round-robin so segment key-ranges fully overlap). fence16 consults per-segment min/max before probing; bloom16 a per-segment blocked Bloom (~10 bits/key, one 64-byte block per query); route16 a global key->segment hash map built at open; k1/fan16/oracle16 are f38's arms re-run so every comparison is same-run
predictions registered in filter-plan.md before the first full run
